title: Social Security Design and Its Political Support
text:
The online appendix
This online appendix accompanies Social Security Design and Its Political Support by Rasmus K. S. Berg and Martín Gonzalez-Eiras. It extends the paper’s three quantitative sections, on Argentina’s pension reform, on the rich economies with the pension design given and on the endogenous design. It shows the results across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity, the UK compared with the U.S., the alternative calibration of the taste for leisure, a second cost of redistribution, and the paths behind the paper’s readings in a single year. Every number is built by the paper’s own pipeline from the model’s results; none is typed.

The coverage reform of section 5.

title: A. Argentina
text:
Section 5 of the paper calibrates the model with informal households to Argentina before its coverage reforms and reads the reforms as a rise of the universal pension ε; appendix E gives the household survey and the identification. This part shows how the equilibrium depends on the whole pension design, how the reform and the calibration depend on the intertemporal elasticity of substitution (IES), and what changes when the taste for leisure is identified quartile by quartile.

A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria: the equilibrium in 2010 over a grid of designs (ε, θ), with the reform as a move across it.
A2. The intertemporal elasticity of substitution: the calibration and the reform’s paths in levels at each IES of the grid.
A3. Identification of X: the paper’s common taste for leisure against one per quartile.

title: A1. How pension designs shape the equilibria
text:
Each point of the figure is an economy that has always had one pension design, the universal pension ε on the horizontal axis and the Bismarckian index θ in the color, read in 2010 under log preferences; every other parameter is the paper’s calibration. A higher universal pension raises the equilibrium tax rate and lowers the savings rate, the workweek and the savings of informal relative to formal households. A more Bismarckian design lowers the tax rate and raises the savings rate and the workweek. The black line is the calibrated θ, and its two markers are the pre-reform ε and the universal level the reform installs. Between them the tax rate rises by more than the reform raises it on impact in section 5: here informal households have always saved under the universal system, while on impact the retirees of 2010 hold savings made under the old one. The rise between the markers is close to the reform’s effect in 2040, once those savings have adjusted.
\(\cdot\)

title: A2. The intertemporal elasticity of substitution
text:
Argentina’s calibration across the intertemporal elasticity
The paper’s benchmark is log preferences, and figure 5.2 reports the reform across the IES ρ. Each ρ is calibrated anew to the same targets, so a change of ρ moves the calibrated parameters as well as the curvature of utility. This page shows both.
Four panels are parameters solved jointly with the equilibrium path at each ρ, and two are predictions of the calibration, the savings rate and the informal savings ratio in 2010. The discount factor and the political weight of the old both fall as the IES rises. The second falls because the young resist taxation less, so a lighter weight of the old reproduces the observed tax rate. At the lowest elasticities of the grid the thirty-year discount factor exceeds one. The savings rate falls with the IES and the informal savings ratio rises, while the informal productivity and taste for leisure barely move.
\(\cdot\)

title: A3. Identification of X
text:
The calibration
The paper takes the taste for leisure \(X\) common to the four formal income quartiles and pins its level by the average formal workweek, so that relative hours across the quartiles are a prediction. The alternative takes the survey’s relative hours as data and identifies one \(X_i\) per quartile, which leaves the level of hours unidentified. The two calibrations share their targets, \(\beta\), \(\omega\) and every equilibrium outcome of section 5: the tax rate, savings, hours in efficiency units and the reform at every ρ. The reason is that the productivity distribution reaches the aggregates only through \(\sum_{i>0}\gamma_i\eta_i^{1+\xi}/X_i^{\xi}\), which both calibrations normalize to one (appendix E). The tables below therefore show only what differs.
Four rows of the paper’s calibration table differ. In the survey, hours rise less with income than the common \(X\) predicts: the top quartile works fewer hours than predicted, as section 5 notes, and the others a little more. The vector \(X_i\) take those hours as data, so the taste for leisure rises with income, and the productivities spread further apart to reproduce the same relative incomes. The informal productivity and taste for leisure are measured against the formal average and move with it.
\(\cdot\)

title: A3. Identification of X
text:
Why the level of \(X\) differs
The level of the taste for leisure is not comparable across the two calibrations. Under the common \(X\) it is the unit in which hours are measured: it is set so that average formal hours in the model equal the observed workweek, and every productivity scales with it. Under the vector \(X_i\) the survey’s relative hours fix only the ratios of the \(X_i\), and the unit of hours is a normalization, which sets the level of every \(X_i\), of the productivities and of the informal taste for leisure. Since that level enters no aggregate, nothing else moves. Across the IES, the common \(X\) falls a little as ρ rises, because average hours are matched against a slightly different equilibrium at each ρ, while the informal parameters barely move under either calibration.
\(\cdot\)

title: B. Rich OECD countries with the design given
text:
Section 6 of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S., the UK and France and changes the U.S. calibration one characteristic at a time: its pension design, its demography, and the income distribution, voting patterns and taste for leisure that set France apart. Appendix F gives the data and the household heterogeneity. This part shows the calibrations across the IES, the counterfactuals with the UK compared with the U.S. and with the UK regrouped at the U.S. income groups, the U.S. counterfactuals across the Frisch elasticity, and what changes when the taste for leisure is identified group by group.

B1. Calibration: the three calibrations at every IES of the grid.
B2. Other countries: what shapes pensions, savings and labor supply in the U.S. and the UK, and the UK at the U.S. income groups.
B3. Other parameters: the U.S. counterfactuals across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity.
B4. Identification of X: the common taste for leisure against one per income group.
crumbs: B. Rich OECD countries with the design given

title: B1. Calibration
text:
The calibrations across the intertemporal elasticity
Each country is calibrated at every ρ of the grid against its own targets. The discount factor is calibrated on the U.S. and imposed on the UK and France, so their interest factors are predictions. The political weight of the old falls as the IES rises in every country, since the young resist taxation less, and it keeps its ranking: highest in the U.S., close behind in France, lowest in the UK. The savings rate falls with the IES in every country, and the UK’s and France’s interest factors rise toward the U.S. target. The taste for leisure, pinned by each country’s average workweek, falls a little with the IES in the UK and France and is nearly flat in the U.S. At the lowest elasticities of the grid the thirty-year discount factor exceeds one, which the UK and France inherit.
\(\cdot\)

title: B2. Other countries
text:
What shapes pensions, savings and labor supply in the U.S. and the UK
The figure repeats the paper’s figure 6.1 for the U.S. and, below it on the same axis, for the UK. Each host keeps its own calibration and changes one characteristic over the whole horizon. The characteristics are its design, moved to the two corners; its population growth, halved (mild ageing) or set to zero (acute ageing); or France’s income distribution, voting patterns or taste for leisure, with France’s households cut at the host’s income percentiles. On both hosts ageing and the design move the tax rate most, except on the U.S. at an IES of two, where France’s voting patterns move it by more than either corner of the design. Ageing and France’s voting patterns move the UK’s tax rate by less than the U.S. one at every IES. Flat benefits raise it by less up to an IES of one, while fully earnings-related ones lower it by more at every IES. Two rows change sign between the hosts. France’s income distribution raises the UK’s tax rate where it lowers the U.S. one, because at the UK’s income cuts France is the more unequal of the two (appendix F). France’s taste for leisure lengthens the UK’s workweek where it shortens the U.S. one, since France’s average taste for leisure lies between the two hosts’.

title: B2. Other countries
section: The UK at U.S. income groups
text:
The UK at U.S. income groups
The paper cuts the UK’s households at the UK’s own income groups, which identify θ from the replacement rates at half-mean and mean income. It cuts France at the U.S. percentiles, so that its households replace the U.S. ones type by type, and regroups France at the UK’s cuts for the UK as host. The table sets the groupings side by side. Regrouping changes what the calibration reads: θ is read off the replacement rates at other cuts, ω follows, and the productivity spread is that of other groups. At the U.S. cuts the UK’s productivity spread is much narrower than at its own, while France’s at the UK’s cuts is wider than at the U.S. ones. The UK at the U.S. cuts is a linear fit of the UK’s group means against cumulative population shares rather than a recount of the survey, so its spread is an approximation. The tabs give the two regroupings group by group.
\(\cdot\)

title: B3. Other parameters
text:
The U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity
The figure shows the counterfactuals of section 6 on the U.S. across the two elasticities that govern the households’ responses. The intertemporal elasticity ρ varies at the paper’s Frisch elasticity; the Frisch elasticity ξ varies under log preferences. At each ξ the U.S. and France are recalibrated to the same targets, so the discount factor, the political weight of the old and the taste for leisure take new values. The ranking of the determinants holds at every ξ of the grid: ageing and the design move the tax rate most, France’s characteristics far less. A higher Frisch elasticity dampens the responses of the tax rate a little and some responses of savings by more, and it enlarges every response of hours, since labor supply is more elastic.

title: B4. Identification of X
text:
The calibration
As for Argentina (A3), the paper takes the taste for leisure \(X\) common to the income groups and pins its level by each country’s average workweek; the alternative identifies one \(X_i\) per group from the observed relative hours. In every country the two calibrations share the discount factor, the political weight of the old, the tax rate, savings and aggregate hours. They also share every counterfactual that changes neither the productivities nor the taste for leisure: the design, ageing and France’s voting patterns. The tables and the figure show only what differs.
Two rows of the paper’s calibration table differ, the taste for leisure and the productivity spread. Under the vector \(X_i\) the taste for leisure rises with income in all three countries: observed hours rise less with income than the common \(X\) predicts, the high group working fewer hours than predicted. To reproduce the same relative incomes with those hours, the productivity spread widens.
\(\cdot\)
Group by group, the vector \(X_i\) are a fraction of the common \(X\), and their level carries no information of its own. Under the common \(X\) the level is the unit of hours: it is set so that the model’s average workweek is the observed one, relative to the U.S. for the UK and France, and the productivities scale with it. Under the vector \(X_i\) the relative hours fix only the ratios of the \(X_i\), and the unit is a normalization. That is why the level differs so much between the two while every aggregate is the same.
\(\cdot\)

title: B4. Identification of X
text:
The counterfactuals that differ
France’s income distribution is imposed through the productivities and its leisure preferences through the taste for leisure, so these are the rows the treatment of leisure moves, with the row that imposes all of France’s characteristics at once. On the U.S. the vector \(X_i\) strengthens the effect of France’s income distribution at every IES and makes that of its leisure preferences on hours a little smaller. On the UK the effect of France’s income distribution on the tax rate changes sign. The vector \(X_i\) read part of the observed income dispersion off relative hours, which are much flatter in the UK than in France, so at the UK’s income cuts France’s productivity spread falls below the UK’s, where under the common \(X\) it lies above.

title: C. Endogenous design
text:
Section 7 of the paper lets the electorate choose the design θ as well as the tax rate, under a deadweight cost of redistribution whose parameter λ is calibrated so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. Appendix C derives the cost and appendix G holds further results. This part follows the design along each country’s projected demography, compares the UK with the U.S., sets a second cost specification against the paper’s, varies the elasticities, and reports the checks of the timing of the choice.

C1. The path in levels: the design, the tax rate, savings and hours as the U.S., the UK and France age, with the design chosen and with it pinned.
C2. Other countries: what shapes the design in the U.S. and the UK.
C3. Other cost specifications: the paper’s cost against a cost attached to the design itself.
C4. Other parameters: the U.S. across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity.
C5. The timing of the choice: the corner the design reaches without the cost, under each timing.

title: C1. The path in levels
text:
By country
The calibration targets the design of 2020 only; every other design along the path is an outcome of the model, chosen one period ahead. The figures follow the three countries from 1990, whose electorate sets the design of 2020, to 2110; the demography is constant from 2080. Each country keeps its own calibration and demography. Its cost parameter is either the one calibrated on the U.S., the cross-country test of appendix G along the path, or its own, the parameter at which its electorate re-elects its observed design. France has no own parameter, since no value of it re-elects France’s fully Bismarckian design.
In every country the chosen design moves against the number of workers per retiree. As the population ages, the electorate ties benefits more closely to earnings, and the design levels off when the demography does. Under the U.S. cost parameter the three countries’ designs keep their observed order in 2020: the UK’s lowest, France’s highest, the U.S. in between. From 2050 the U.S. design lies above France’s, since France’s population is already old in 2020 and ages least afterwards. The UK’s workers per retiree rise until 2020 before they fall, and its design moves against them, falling and then rising. At its own parameter the UK’s design passes through its observed value in 2020 and follows the same pattern. The tax rate rises with ageing everywhere.

title: C2. Other countries
text:
What shapes the pension design in the U.S. and the UK
The figure takes the counterfactuals of the paper’s figure 7.1 to the UK, at the UK’s own cost parameter, and sets it below the U.S. on the same axis. Each counterfactual is read twice, with the design pinned at the host’s observed value and with it chosen. Acute ageing ties both designs more closely to earnings, the UK’s by a little more. France’s voting patterns move both toward flat benefits, the UK’s by about as much at the lowest IES and by less at the higher ones, since its own voting profile is already flatter than the U.S. one. France’s income distribution moves the two designs in opposite directions at every IES: on the U.S. it compresses relative incomes, on the UK it spreads them. On the UK, choosing the design leaves the tax rate, the savings rate and the workweek close to the readings with the design pinned.

title: C3. Other cost specifications
text:
A cost on the design
The paper’s cost of redistribution scales with the size of the system and with the dispersion of relative incomes, so it vanishes when the design redistributes nothing (appendix C). The alternative attaches the cost to the design itself, \(f(\theta) = \phi + (1-\phi)\theta^{p}\), with \(\phi\) imposed and \(p\) calibrated, as λ is, so that the U.S. electorate re-elects its observed design. It charges a flat benefit whatever that benefit redistributes. The table gives the two calibrations.
\(\cdot\)
Under the cost on the design, acute ageing raises the chosen design by less at every IES, since that cost does not grow with the tax rate that ageing raises: by about half as much at an IES of one, the comparison the paper draws, by much less at the lowest IES and by almost as much at the highest. France’s voting patterns move the design further toward flat benefits. France’s income distribution compresses the redistributive stakes but leaves the cost in place, and it takes the design to the Bismarckian corner at every IES.

title: C4. Other parameters
text:
The counterfactuals across the intertemporal and the Frisch elasticity
The figure shows the endogenous design of the U.S. across the intertemporal elasticity ρ, at the paper’s Frisch elasticity, and across the Frisch elasticity ξ, under log preferences. Each value is a separate calibration with its own cost parameter, which falls steeply as the IES rises (table 4 of the paper) and a little as the Frisch elasticity rises. Across the IES the figure holds every counterfactual of the paper’s figure 7.1. Across the Frisch elasticity only acute ageing is computed: the design it leads the electorate to choose is the same at every ξ, while the tax rate rises by less at a higher Frisch elasticity, whether the design is pinned or chosen.

title: C5. The timing of the choice
text:
Appendix C of the paper shows that, without the cost of redistribution and at the U.S. calibration, each of the three timings it examines puts the design at a corner. A design chosen together with the tax rate re-splits benefits that current retirees have already earned. A design chosen one period ahead weighs the young’s stake in redistribution against the forward-looking gain of a more earnings-related system. A design chosen once and for all re-splits current benefits and sets future ones at the same time. The table reports the numerical checks, one block per timing. Chosen with the tax or one period ahead, the design is the Beveridgean corner at every IES checked. Chosen once and for all, it is the Beveridgean corner at the lower elasticities shown and the Bismarckian corner at the higher ones; near the switch the electorate is close to indifferent between the two, so the switch is not sharply located.

title: D2. Numerical checks
text:
References
Section 4 of the paper computes date-specific Markov policy functions by backward induction along the demographic transition, and tests every candidate equilibrium at each state; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) gives the algorithms. The first table compares the date-specific solution with a time-invariant policy function, the approximation of much of the quantitative politico-economic literature, at the same dates. The second counts, for every file of results that records them, the equilibria and the candidates found at any state, and the states at which no candidate passed the test and the solver fell back on ranking the candidates by the integral of the first order condition, the fallback rule of the technical documentation. A single equilibrium at every state means that the selection rule of section 4 never had to choose.

Every table and figure of this appendix is produced by the pipeline in python/paper of the repository, in three stages: the calibrations, the experiments, and a build that reads only their results and writes the exhibits in seconds. REPLICATION.md in the repository maps the data and the code to every output, with the commands and the time each stage takes; the technical documentation (Berg and Gonzalez-Eiras 2026) describes the model, its equilibria and the algorithms. The interactive figures draw from csv files that the build writes from the same results, and each figure’s Data link downloads its file.
The table lists every exhibit of this appendix, the output that holds it, the builder that makes it and the results files it reads; each exhibit’s Source has the same, with the command that rebuilds it.
